current: On the last day of his life, Moses addresses the entire people of Israel in a great farewell speech.
problem: Deuteronomy 1:3 dates the start of the speeches to 1 Shevat; Seder Olam puts Moses' death on 7 Adar, 36 days later. Devarim is not his last day.
evidence: Deut 1:3 'in the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month' https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.1.3 ; Seder Olam Rabbah 10: 'מאחד בשבט ועד ששה באדר, שלשים וששה יום, פירש משה רבינו את כל התורה... בשבעה באדר ... מת' https://www.sefaria.org/Seder_Olam_Rabbah.10
fix: In the last weeks of his life, Moses addresses the entire people of Israel in a great farewell speech.

current: Deuteronomy opens on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year — the Torah is precise: Moses has eleven months to live, or perhaps a single day.
problem: Neither figure fits. The eleventh month is Shevat; by the traditional count Moses died on 7 Adar, the next month, so he has about five weeks left.
evidence: Deut 1:3 https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.1.3 ; Seder Olam Rabbah 10 (1 Shevat to 6 Adar, 36 days; died 7 Adar) https://www.sefaria.org/Seder_Olam_Rabbah.10 ; Rashi on 1:3 'he reproved them only shortly before his death' https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Deuteronomy.1.3
fix: Deuteronomy opens on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year (1:3); by the traditional count in Seder Olam, Moses dies on the seventh day of the next month, Adar, so he has about five weeks to live.

current: the routing of Og of Bashan — whose enormous iron bed was still on display at Rabbah when Deuteronomy was written.
problem: The verse says only that the bedstead 'is now in Rabbah'; 'on display' and 'when Deuteronomy was written' go beyond it and assume a composition date.
evidence: Deut 3:11 'His bedstead, an iron bedstead, is now in Rabbah of the Ammonites; it is nine cubits long' (Heb. הֲלֹה הִוא בְּרַבַּת) https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.3.11
fix: the routing of Og of Bashan, whose iron bedstead, nine cubits long, the text says 'is now in Rabbah of the Ammonites' (3:11).

current: Deuteronomy is sometimes called the 'second Torah' (its Greek name, deutero-nomos, means exactly this) because it repeats and retells so much of what came before — but always with subtle variations that have fascinated scholars.
problem: The Greek name Deuteronomion means 'second law', not 'second Torah'; the transliteration 'deutero-nomos' is also not the name.
evidence: Wikipedia, Book of Deuteronomy: 'Deuteronomy (Ancient Greek: Δευτερονόμιον, romanized: Deuteronómion, lit. "second law")' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Deuteronomy
fix: Deuteronomy's Greek name, Deuteronomion, means 'second law', and the book repeats and retells much of what came before, with variations that have long interested readers.

current: The rabbis solved the problem of discrepancies between Deuteronomy's retelling and the original account by developing the principle that Moses was speaking from his own perspective and memory, while earlier books recorded events from a divine or omniscient perspective.
problem: No rabbinic source states this as a general principle. The Talmud draws a narrower distinction, about the curses only.
evidence: Megillah 31b (cited by Ramban on Lev 26:16): the curses in Leviticus Moses said 'from the mouth of the Almighty', those in Deuteronomy 'from his own mouth' https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.31b ; https://www.sefaria.org/Ramban_on_Leviticus.26.16
fix: The Talmud (Megillah 31b) says Moses spoke the curses of Leviticus as God's words but the curses of Deuteronomy 'on his own', and later commentators used this idea of Moses speaking in his own voice.

current: Similar genres appear in Akkadian literature and in the Egyptian 'Instructions of Amenemhat.'
problem: No Akkadian farewell-address parallel was found or named; the Amenemhat text is a dead king's monologue to his son, which is a fair comparison only if described as such.
evidence: Wikipedia, Instructions of Amenemhat: 'a dramatic monologue delivered by the ghost of the murdered 12th Dynasty pharaoh Amenemhat I to his son Senusret I' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instructions_of_Amenemhat ; biblical farewell speeches: Genesis 49, Joshua 23-24 https://www.sefaria.org/Joshua.23
fix: Similar farewell speeches appear elsewhere in the Bible, such as Jacob's (Genesis 49) and Joshua's (Joshua 23–24), and the Egyptian 'Instructions of Amenemhat' is framed as a dead king's advice to his son.

current: The book's rhetorical style — emotional, repetitive, using the second person singular 'you' as if addressing each listener individually — reflects sophisticated oratorical tradition.
problem: Deuteronomy switches between singular and plural 'you'; 4:1 addresses Israel in the plural (אֶתְכֶם, 'you' plural), while 6:5 uses the singular.
evidence: Deut 4:1 'וְעַתָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל שְׁמַע... אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְלַמֵּד אֶתְכֶם לַעֲשׂוֹת לְמַעַן תִּחְיוּ' https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.4.1 ; Deut 6:5 'וְאָהַבְתָּ... בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ' https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.6.5
fix: The book's style is emotional and repetitive, and it moves between a singular 'you', as if speaking to each listener, and a plural 'you' addressed to the whole people.

current: The geographical details (Sihon's kingdom, Og's bed at Rabbah, the plains of Moab) are consistent with Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age geography.
problem: This is disputed, not settled. Excavations at Tell Hesban, the usual site of Sihon's Heshbon, found no clear 13th-century occupation.
evidence: Wikipedia, Heshbon: 'no trace whatsoever of occupation in the 13th century B.C. ... something was drastically wrong with the biblical story about Heshbon'; LaBianca and Walker report LB/Iron I remains mostly in secondary deposits https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heshbon
fix: Archaeologists debate how well these details fit the Late Bronze Age: excavations at Tell Hesban, the usual site of Sihon's capital Heshbon, found little or no clear occupation from the 13th century BCE.

current: means that returning to Devarim each fall — just before Rosh Hashana — gives the yearly Torah reading the structure of Moses's own life: beginning with creation and ending with death, then beginning again.
problem: Devarim is always read on the Shabbat before Tisha B'Av, in midsummer; Nitzavim, not Devarim, is read just before Rosh Hashana.
evidence: Shulchan Arukh OC 428:4: 'תשעה באב קודם ואתחנן, אתם נצבים קודם ר"ה' https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Orach_Chayim.428.4
fix: means that Devarim is read each midsummer, on the Shabbat before Tisha B'Av, and the rest of Deuteronomy is read over the following weeks, so the yearly cycle begins with creation and ends with Moses's death, then begins again.

current: Moses describes his personal anguish: he pleaded with God many times to be allowed to cross the Jordan and see the good land, and God refused, forbidding him even to mention the subject again.
problem: The verse says only 'I pleaded'; 'many times' comes from midrash (Devarim Rabbah 11:10 says a decree was issued ten times), not the text.
evidence: Deut 3:23-26 'וָאֶתְחַנַּן... אַל תּוֹסֶף דַּבֵּר אֵלַי עוֹד' https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.3.23 ; Devarim Rabbah 11:10 'as many as ten times it was decreed against him' https://www.sefaria.org/Devarim_Rabbah.11.10
fix: Moses describes his personal anguish: he pleaded with God to be allowed to cross the Jordan and see the good land, and God refused, forbidding him even to mention the subject again (3:23–26).

current: The Ten Commandments are repeated in full but with one important change: the Exodus version says 'remember' (zachor) the Sabbath; Deuteronomy says 'guard' (shamor) — and adds that servants and animals must rest because Israel was a slave in Egypt.
problem: There are several differences between the versions (e.g. 'false witness' שקר vs שוא, the order of house and wife in the last commandment); and Exodus also lists servants and animals among those who rest. What Deuteronomy adds is the Egypt reason.
evidence: Exodus 20:10 includes 'your male or female slave, or your cattle' https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.20.10 ; Deut 5:14-15 'so that your male and female slave may rest as you do. Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt' https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.5.14 ; Deut 5:17-18 vs Exodus 20:13-14 https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.5.17
fix: The Ten Commandments are repeated with some differences; the best known is that Exodus says 'remember' (zachor) the Sabbath and Deuteronomy says 'observe' (shamor), and Deuteronomy gives a new reason for the Sabbath rest: so your servants may rest as you do, remembering that you were a slave in Egypt (5:12–15).

current: The Shema — three words in Hebrew — is the most fundamental declaration in Judaism
problem: The Shema verse has six Hebrew words.
evidence: Deut 6:4 'שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד' https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.6.4

current: The second word 'Echad' (One) is written with an enlarged letter dalet in Torah scrolls — because the word looks similar to another word (acher — 'other'), and mistakenly reading 'hear, our God is other' would be theologically catastrophic.
problem: Echad is the sixth word, not the second. The enlarged ayin of Shema is also omitted; the reason given is one tradition, not a documented fact.
evidence: Deut 6:4 (Echad is the last of six words) https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.6.4 ; Wikipedia, Shema: 'There are two larger-print letters in the first sentence ('ayin ע and daleth ד) which, when combined, spell "עד"' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shema_Yisrael
fix: The last word, 'Echad' (One), is written with an enlarged dalet, and the first word, 'Shema', with an enlarged ayin; together the two letters spell ed, 'witness'.

current: The rabbis calculate that the Hebrew word for 'very' (me'od) in 'love God with all your very' is an anagram for 'money' (mamaon) — loving God with all one's might means with one's resources.
problem: No anagram is involved (the letters don't match). The Mishnah simply interprets 'with all your might' as 'with all your money'.
evidence: Mishnah Berakhot 9:5 'וּבְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ, בְּכָל מָמוֹנֶךָ' https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Berakhot.9.5
fix: The Mishnah (Berakhot 9:5) reads 'with all your might' (me'odekha) as 'with all your money', so loving God includes how one uses one's resources.

current: The Shema's declaration is a polemic against this understanding: not 'our God is the strongest' but 'YHWH is uniquely one, undivided, without peer.'
problem: This is one reading presented as fact. The phrase can also mean 'the LORD alone' is Israel's God; Rashi reads it as 'the LORD, now our God, will in the future be the one LORD' of all nations.
evidence: Rashi on 6:4 'ה' שֶׁהוּא אֱלֹהֵינוּ עַתָּה, וְלֹא אֱלֹהֵי הָאֻמּוֹת, הוּא עָתִיד לִהְיוֹת ה' אֶחָד' https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Deuteronomy.6.4

current: The mezuzah — a scroll containing the Shema and Ve'ahavta in a case affixed to every doorpost — is one of Judaism's most universal home practices

evidence: Shulchan Arukh YD 288:1 'כותבין שתי פרשיות שמע והיה אם שמוע' https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Yoreh_De'ah.288.1

current: The law of worship centralization — all sacrifice must happen at the 'chosen place' — was the most significant religious reform in Israelite history, and its implementation is described in detail in 2 Kings 22-23 under King Josiah (c. 621 BCE). Josiah's sweeping destruction of provincial shrines, the Asherah poles, and the high places followed almost exactly the prescription of this portion, which many scholars believe was the 'book of the law' discovered in the Temple during his reign. Before centralization, worship at local shrines was commonplace and largely accepted — after Deuteronomy, it became the paradigmatic sin of every king who 'did not remove the high places.'
problem: Superlative is unsourced; the scholarly identification is stated partly as fact; and the chronology is confused: the Book of Kings faults kings long before Josiah (Asa, Jehoshaphat) for not removing the high places.
evidence: 2 Kings 22:8 'I have found a scroll of the Teaching in the House of GOD' https://www.sefaria.org/II_Kings.22.8 ; 1 Kings 15:14 'The shrines, indeed, were not abolished' (Asa) https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings.15.14 ; 1 Kings 22:44 (Jehoshaphat) https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings.22.44 ; Wikipedia, Josiah: 'Book of the Law (likely an early version of the Book of Deuteronomy)' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah
fix: 2 Kings 22–23 describes King Josiah (late 7th century BCE) destroying the high places and Asherah poles after a 'scroll of the Teaching' was found in the Temple (22:8), and many scholars identify that scroll with an early form of Deuteronomy. The Book of Kings judges earlier kings by the same standard, faulting even Asa and Jehoshaphat because 'the shrines were not abolished' (1 Kings 15:14; 22:44).

current: operated through the 8th century BCE before being deliberately decommissioned, likely as part of the Hezekianic and Josianic reforms.
problem: Linking the end of the Arad shrine to Josiah's reform reflects Aharoni's older dating; the current strata dating (Herzog's low chronology) puts the fortress sequence in the 8th century and the shrine's end is usually tied to Hezekiah. No source found supporting a Josianic phase.
evidence: Wikipedia, Tel Arad: 'Herzog's 2002 interim report adopts the now better accepted "low chronology"'; strata IX–VIII second half of 8th century BCE https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Arad
fix: was in use in the 8th century BCE and was later deliberately put out of use; its excavators linked this to the religious reforms of the kings of Judah.

current: troubled the Talmud deeply because the Torah attaches the same reward to it as to honoring parents: 'that it may go well with you and your days be long.' This juxtaposition led to one of the Talmud's most famous discussions (Berakhot 33b) about whether we can know the reasons for commandments, and eventually to the Mishnah's ruling (Berakhot 5:3) that a prayer leader who says 'Your mercy extends to a bird's nest' is silenced, because it implies God has a reason for the commandment — a presumption the rabbis rejected.
problem: The causal chain is invented and reversed: the Mishnah (Berakhot 5:3) is earlier than the Gemara (33b), and 33b is not about the equal reward. The Gemara gives two explanations: the prayer breeds jealousy among creatures, or it makes God's decrees into expressions of mercy.
evidence: Mishnah Berakhot 5:3 'הָאוֹמֵר עַל קַן צִפּוֹר יַגִּיעוּ רַחֲמֶיךָ... מְשַׁתְּקִין אוֹתוֹ' https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Berakhot.5.3 ; Berakhot 33b: 'one said ... he engenders jealousy among God's creations... one said ... he transforms the attributes of the Holy One into expressions of mercy, when they are nothing but decrees' https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.33b
fix: carries the same reward as honoring parents: 'that you may fare well and have a long life' (22:7; compare 5:16). Separately, the Mishnah (Berakhot 5:3) rules that a prayer leader who says 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest' is silenced, and the Talmud (Berakhot 33b) explains that he presents God's commandments as mercy when they are decrees.

current: Ki Teitzei is the source of one of Judaism's most discussed ethical concepts: kibbud av va'em (honoring father and mother) and shilu'ach ha-ken (the mother bird) sharing identical rewards, teaching that we cannot rank commandments by importance. The Talmudic school of Ben Azzai (Avot 4:2) derived from this the principle: 'run to perform a minor commandment as you would a major one, for you do not know the reward of the commandments.'
